name: STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy

clinicalPearls: A monogenic type I interferonopathy caused by gain-of-function variants in STING1 (TMEM173), usually autosomal dominant and frequently arising de novo.
Presents in early infancy with systemic inflammation, recurrent fevers and failure to thrive.
Hallmark acral vasculopathy affects cold-exposed sites (fingertips, toes, nose, ears and cheeks), progressing from violaceous plaques to ulceration, necrosis and digital loss.
Destructive nasal disease with septal perforation can closely mimic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Progressive interstitial lung disease is a major cause of morbidity and can culminate in pulmonary fibrosis and respiratory failure.
A strongly positive blood interferon signature supports the diagnosis, while positive autoantibodies (ANA, ANCA) frequently cause diagnostic confusion.
Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors that block downstream interferon signalling are the mainstay; conventional corticosteroids and cytotoxic immunosuppression are typically inadequate.
Cold exposure characteristically exacerbates the cutaneous vasculopathy.
reference.pathophysiology: STING (stimulator of interferon genes), encoded by STING1/TMEM173, is an endoplasmic reticulum adaptor that normally senses cyclic dinucleotides generated by the cytosolic DNA sensor cGAS. Gain-of-function variants lock STING in a constitutively active conformation independent of its ligand, driving persistent TBK1-IRF3 activation and unrestrained transcription of type I interferons, predominantly interferon-beta. The resulting chronic interferon signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway upregulates interferon-stimulated genes in endothelium, leucocytes and lung, producing small-vessel inflammation, microthrombosis and tissue ischaemia that manifest as the characteristic acral vasculopathy and interstitial lung disease. Sustained interferon exposure also promotes a breach of self-tolerance with autoantibody production and T-cell cytopenia, explaining the frequent overlap with systemic autoimmune disease and the diagnostic confusion with vasculitis and lupus.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other ANCA-associated vasculitides
Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome and other type I interferonopathies
Systemic lupus erythematosus with cutaneous vasculopathy or chilblain lupus
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing for STING1 (TMEM173) variants
Blood interferon signature (interferon-stimulated gene expression score)
High-resolution CT of the chest for interstitial lung disease
Skin biopsy of affected acral lesions showing small-vessel vasculopathy and microthrombi
Autoantibody panel including ANA, ANCA and antiphospholipid antibodies
Pulmonary function testing including gas transfer
redFlags: Progressive digital ischaemia, necrosis or gangrene threatening tissue loss
Rapidly worsening breathlessness or hypoxia suggesting progressive interstitial lung disease
Nasal septal perforation or destructive midface involvement
Failure to thrive with unremitting systemic inflammation in an infant
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and depends largely on the severity of interstitial lung disease, which is the principal determinant of mortality. Early JAK inhibition may stabilise disease, but established pulmonary fibrosis and digital loss are often irreversible.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the disease as ANCA-associated vasculitis or lupus because of positive autoantibodies with nasal and pulmonary involvement.
Expecting conventional corticosteroids and cytotoxic immunosuppression to control disease, which they rarely do.
Overlooking early interstitial lung disease when respiratory symptoms are still mild.
Attributing acral lesions to primary Raynaud phenomenon or frostbite.
references: Paediatric rheumatology and clinical immunology textbooks
Autoinflammatory disease and interferonopathy reference sources
Inborn errors of immunity reference sources
management: JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, ruxolitinib or tofacitinib) as targeted therapy to block type I interferon JAK-STAT signalling, as conventional immunosuppression is often inadequate
Supportive wound care for acral ulceration and necrosis, with cold-avoidance measures and protection of the extremities
Monitor and manage interstitial lung disease with serial high-resolution CT and pulmonary function including gas transfer, this being the chief determinant of outcome
Vasodilator and antiplatelet measures to limit digital ischaemia and preserve tissue
Genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant, frequently de novo, STING1 variant with family assessment
Multidisciplinary care across clinical immunology, rheumatology, respiratory medicine and dermatology
Escalate early for respiratory failure and consider lung transplantation assessment in end-stage pulmonary fibrosis
